_about: Written for ErrorGeek in our own words (GPL-3.0). 'codes' fills in common codes that no open source header lists (Configuration Manager, Intune, Windows servicing). 'hints' are short fix tips, keyed by the 8 digit hex form (Win32 codes use their 0x8007xxxx form).

87D00213: Configuration Manager: the operation timed out. For a deployment this often means the install ran longer than its maximum allowed run time.
87D00215: Configuration Manager: the item was not found.
87D00314: Configuration Manager: timed out getting the version information for a configuration item (the client could not get the policy or content details in time).
87D00324: Configuration Manager: the application installed, but the detection method did not find it afterwards.
87D00325: Configuration Manager: the application uninstalled, but the detection method still finds it.
87D00607: Configuration Manager: content not found. The client could not get a content location for the package.
87D00664: Configuration Manager: the software updates job was cancelled.
87D00668: Configuration Manager: the software update is still needed after it was installed.
87D00669: Configuration Manager: the client could not get content locations for the software updates at this time.
87D00692: Configuration Manager: Group Policy conflict. A local or domain policy is overriding the Windows Update settings the client needs.
87D01106: Configuration Manager: could not check the program file or build its command line.
87D1041C: Intune: the app installed, but the detection rule did not find it afterwards.
800F081F: Windows servicing: the source files for the feature or package could not be found.
800F0831: Windows servicing: the component store is missing something the update needs, often an earlier update.
800F0906: Windows servicing: the source files could not be downloaded.
800F0907: Windows servicing: Group Policy stopped Windows from downloading the source files.
800F0922: Windows servicing: an installer inside the package failed while the update or feature was being applied.

hints.80070005: Run the tool or command as administrator. Check NTFS, share and registry permissions for the account doing the work. Antivirus or Controlled Folder Access can also block it.
hints.80070002: A file the program expected is missing. Check the path and that the source files are complete. For Windows Update, renaming the SoftwareDistribution folder (with the service stopped) often clears it.
hints.80070003: The folder in the path does not exist. Check for typos, mapped drives that are not connected in this session, and paths that only exist for another user.
hints.80004005: This is a catch-all failure, so the code alone says little. Check the program's own log for the line just before the error.
hints.8007000E: Close other programs or add memory. On a server, look for a process leaking memory in Task Manager or Performance Monitor.
hints.80070020: Another process has the file open. Close it, or use Resource Monitor (CPU tab, Associated Handles) to find which process holds it. Antivirus scans are a common cause.
hints.80070057: A setting, switch or value passed to the program is wrong. Check the command line or script for typos and unsupported options.
hints.80070070: Free up space on the drive being written to, including the system drive and temp folders.
hints.800705B4: Something did not answer in time. Check network links, slow storage and whether the remote service is running.
hints.80070643: A Windows Installer (MSI) package failed. Run it again with msiexec /l*v log.txt and search the log for "return value 3" to find the action that failed.
hints.80070652: Another installation is already running. Wait for it to finish, or restart, then try again. Check for a stuck msiexec.exe in Task Manager.
hints.80070653: Windows Installer could not open the package. Check the path, that the file copied in full and that the account can read it.
hints.80070BC2: The install worked, but a restart is needed to finish it.
hints.80070669: The install worked and the installer has started a restart.
hints.8007052E: The user name or password is wrong, or the account cannot be used here. Check the account, the domain prefix and any saved credentials.
hints.800706BA: The remote computer did not answer the RPC call. Check that it is on, that DNS resolves the right address, that the firewall allows RPC and that the service you need is running.
hints.8007051F: No domain controller answered. Check DNS settings on the client, network access to a domain controller and the computer's time.
hints.8007054B: The domain name could not be found. Check that the client uses your internal DNS servers, not a public one.
hints.80070035: The network path could not be found. Check the name resolves, the share exists, file sharing is on and SMB is allowed through the firewall.
hints.80070043: The share name does not exist on that server. Check the spelling and that the share is still published.
hints.80070775: The account is locked out. Unlock it in Active Directory, then find the device or service still using an old password.
hints.80070532: The password has expired. Change it, then update any services or scheduled tasks that use it.
hints.80070422: The service is disabled. Set its start type back to Manual or Automatic in services.msc, then start it.
hints.8007042C: A service it depends on did not start. Check the Dependencies tab in services.msc and start those first.
hints.8007041D: The service did not respond in time when starting. Check the System event log for the reason.
hints.80073712: The component store is damaged. Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow, then try the update again.
hints.8007232B: The DNS name does not exist. For KMS activation, check the _vlmcs._tcp SRV record exists in DNS, or point the client at the host with slmgr /skms.
hints.80072EE2: The connection timed out. Check internet or WSUS access, the proxy and the firewall.
hints.80072EE7: The server name did not resolve. Check DNS and the proxy settings (netsh winhttp show proxy).
hints.80072EFD: Could not connect to the server. Check the firewall, the proxy and that the server is up on that port.
hints.80072F8F: A secure (TLS) connection failed. Check the clock and time zone, the root certificates and the TLS versions allowed on both ends.
hints.8024402C: Check DNS and the WinHTTP proxy (netsh winhttp show proxy). On WSUS clients, check the server name in the WUServer policy is correct.
hints.80244022: On WSUS, the WsusPool application pool in IIS has usually stopped. Start it, and if it keeps stopping, raise its Private Memory Limit.
hints.80244019: The update server returned 404. Check the WSUS address and port in policy, and that the WSUS content folder and virtual directories are intact.
hints.80244017: The proxy or server wants a login the update agent cannot give. Allow the update URLs through the proxy without authentication.
hints.80244018: The proxy or server refused the request. Allow the Windows Update or WSUS URLs through the proxy and firewall.
hints.8024401C: The update server took too long to answer. Check the server load, the WSUS database and the network path.
hints.80240438: The update service could not be reached. Check internet access, the proxy and policies that block Windows Update.
hints.8024002E: A policy blocks the client from going to Windows Update directly. Check "Do not connect to any Windows Update Internet locations" and the WSUS settings.
hints.80240022: Every update in the batch failed. Look at the result code of each update in WindowsUpdate.log (Get-WindowsUpdateLog) to find the real cause.
hints.80240017: The update does not apply to this device: wrong edition, wrong architecture, a missing prerequisite or it is already installed.
hints.800F081F: Point Windows at a source: DISM /Online /Enable-Feature with /Source:wim:path\install.wim:1 /LimitAccess using media that matches the build. Or set the "Specify settings for optional component installation" policy so it can use Windows Update.
hints.800F0831: Install the missing earlier update (the CBS.log names it), or run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then retry.
hints.800F0906: Check internet access, or use local media with /Source. On WSUS clients, allow optional component downloads from Windows Update in policy.
hints.800F0907: Set the "Specify settings for optional component installation and component repair" policy so the device may download from Windows Update, or use a local /Source.
hints.800F0922: Check CBS.log for the failing step. Common causes: a full System Reserved or EFI partition, a VPN or proxy blocking the download, or a stuck .NET Framework install.
hints.800F0954: Often seen when installing optional features (such as .NET 3.5 or RSAT) on a WSUS client. Let the device use Windows Update for optional features in policy, or install from local media.
hints.C0000005: The program read or wrote memory it should not. Update or reinstall the program and its drivers, then check the Application event log for the faulting module.
hints.C000006D: The sign-in failed. Check the user name, domain and password, and that the clocks on client and server match.
hints.C000006A: The password was wrong. Reset it, then update any saved credentials, services and mapped drives that still use the old one.
hints.C0000234: The account is locked out. Unlock it, then use the lockout source (event 4740 on a domain controller) to find what keeps sending the old password.
hints.C0000072: The account is disabled. Enable it in Active Directory or Computer Management.
hints.C0000071: The password has expired. Change it and update anything that uses it.
hints.C0000064: The user name does not exist. Check the spelling and the domain.
hints.C0000193: The account has expired. Change the expiry date on the account.
hints.C000015B: The user has not been granted this type of sign-in. Check the user rights assignment policies, such as "Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services".
hints.800B0109: The certificate chains to a root that is not trusted. Import the root certificate into the Trusted Root store, or fix the chain on the server.
hints.800B0101: A certificate has expired or the clock is wrong. Check the date and time, then renew the certificate.
hints.87D00213: If the install takes longer than the deployment type's maximum allowed run time, raise that setting. Check AppEnforce.log for the process that was still running.
hints.87D00314: Trigger the Machine Policy Retrieval cycle and retry. Check CIAgent.log and CIDownloader.log, and that the client can reach its management point.
hints.87D00324: Check the detection method matches what the installer really writes (product code, file version or registry value, and 32 or 64 bit paths). AppEnforce.log shows the install exit code and the detection result.
hints.87D00325: The uninstall ran but left behind what the detection method looks for. Fix the uninstall command or the detection method, then check AppEnforce.log.
hints.87D00607: Make sure the content is distributed to a distribution point in the client's boundary group, and that the boundaries cover the client. Check ContentTransferManager.log, CAS.log and LocationServices.log.
hints.87D00664: The updates job was cancelled, often by a restart, a maintenance window ending or a newer deployment. Check UpdatesHandler.log and run a new evaluation.
hints.87D00668: The update installed but still shows as needed. Restart the device, then check WUAHandler.log, UpdatesHandler.log and WindowsUpdate.log.
hints.87D00669: Check the update package is distributed to a distribution point in the client's boundary group, and that the deployment allows a fallback source if needed. Check LocationServices.log.
hints.87D00692: Check WUAHandler.log, then run gpresult /h to find the GPO that sets the WSUS server or Windows Update settings and conflicts with the ConfigMgr client.
hints.87D01106: Check the program command line, that the file exists in the content and that the deployment type points at the right file. AppEnforce.log shows the full command it tried.
hints.87D1041C: Check the app's detection rule matches what the installer really writes (path, version, registry key or MSI product code), including 32 or 64 bit locations. The IntuneManagementExtension.log shows the result.
